You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 4 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 4 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

structured_output.failure_statement: The agent silently drifts from an execution/environment constraint the user set at the start of the task — working in the wrong branch/workspace, or violating a stated no-network rule — instead of confirming it's still operating within that constraint and asking before deviating.

remedy_content.heading: Environment & Execution Constraints
remedy_content.text: When the user states an execution constraint at the start of a task (target branch/workspace, no-network, or another environment rule), treat it as fixed for the whole task, not just the first step. Before acting, confirm you're still in the stated branch/workspace; if something would force a deviation (e.g. you think you need network access), stop and ask rather than silently changing the plan.

structured_output.routing_rationale: All six incidents are ignored-instruction failures where the fix is "hold the line on a constraint the user already stated" — no multi-step procedure is needed, so skill is overkill, and the constraints (which branch, whether network is allowed, which files are off-limits) are per-task and stated in conversation, not statically known, so a generic hook can't check them mechanically. A one/two-line standing claude-md rule is the cheapest fix. The evidence splits into two distinct concrete failure targets: (a) deviating from a stated execution/environment constraint (wrong branch/workspace, no-network) set at task start, which matches existing pending proposal R4's "wrong branch/workspace" theme and should revise it rather than sibling it; and (b) expanding the scope of an edit beyond what was authorized (touching declared off-limits files, rebuilding more than a requested minimal change, skipping a mandated workflow step like a changelog) — a different mechanism (scope creep vs. wrong environment) with no existing remedy, so it gets its own proposal. Both halves partition all 6 promoted incidents exactly once.

dedup.reason: R1 targets verifying completion claims before reporting done. These incidents are about exceeding authorized edit scope, not about falsely claiming verification happened.
R2 is specifically about running a declared verification command before claiming a fake release complete; unrelated to scope-of-edit boundaries.

R3 is framed around unauthorized deletion of content, a destructive-action failure. Incidents 4, 8, and 24 involve modifying or adding beyond scope (changing a formatter, touching tests, rebuilding UI), which is the opposite direction (expansion, not deletion), and incident 31 is a missing required step, not a deletion.

R4 concerns acting in the wrong branch/workspace. These incidents occur within the correct workspace but exceed the authorized scope of the edit or skip a required step — a different concrete failure.

split.failure_statement: The agent expands a change beyond what the user explicitly authorized — editing files declared off-limits, doing more than the requested minimal/targeted edit, or skipping a workflow step mandated by repo policy — instead of checking the diff against the stated scope before calling the work done.

remedy_content.heading: Scope Discipline
remedy_content.text: When the user gives an explicit scope constraint — files/areas not to touch, a minimal or targeted edit only, or a required step mandated by repo policy (e.g. a changelog entry) — treat it as a hard boundary. Before reporting the change done, check your diff against it: don't touch declared off-limits files, don't do more than the requested edit, and don't skip a required step. If a deviation seems necessary, ask first instead of expanding scope silently.

split.routing_rationale: Incidents 4, 8, 24, and 31 share a distinct mechanism from the branch/workspace incidents above: the agent doesn't drift to the wrong environment, it exceeds the authorized scope of the edit itself (touching a file declared off-limits, rebuilding far more than a requested minimal change, or skipping a workflow step like a changelog mandated by repo policy). No existing remedy targets this, and it's simple enough to be a standing rule rather than a skill or hook, since the specific off-limits files/scope aren't known ahead of time by any static check.
